title: Linux - Shell Startup, Aliases, and History
html:
Shell Startup, Aliases, and History

A shell command may behave differently from the executable with the same name if an alias, function, startup file, or environment variable changes how it runs. Check these before trusting a command's output or assuming a script uses the same PATH as an interactive session.

Inspect the current shell

printf '%s\n' "$SHELL" "$PATH"
type -a ls sudo curl 2>/dev/null
alias
command -V python3
history | tail -50

type and command -V reveal whether a name resolves to an alias, function, builtin, or file. command -v and which may not tell the same story for aliases and functions. Shell history can expose commands or credentials, but it may be incomplete, disabled, or held in memory until the session exits.

A modified .bashrc can define a sudo alias that imitates a password prompt, records the response, and passes it to the real command. This can conceal credential interception without changing the sudo executable or PATH.[5] The shell must read the modified startup file and expand the alias.[7] By default, non-interactive Bash does not expand aliases unless expand_aliases is enabled.[6]

Review startup and history files

ls -la ~/.bashrc ~/.bash_profile ~/.profile ~/.zshrc ~/.zprofile ~/.bash_history ~/.zsh_history 2>/dev/null
ls -ld /etc/profile /etc/profile.d /etc/bash.bashrc 2>/dev/null
printenv HISTFILE HISTSIZE HISTCONTROL BASH_ENV ENV 2>/dev/null

A user-writable startup file can execute commands on a future shell launch. A system-wide startup file or a privileged user's startup file is more sensitive if a lower-privileged account can modify it. Non-interactive Bash can also read the file named by BASH_ENV; the environment variables page explains that behavior and other interpreter hooks. Verify which files the actual shell reads for login, interactive, and non-interactive sessions before claiming a persistence path.

Also inspect files sourced by a global startup file. For example, a literal source /opt/app/venv/bin/activate in /etc/bash.bashrc runs the activation file as shell code when a shell actually reads that startup file. Review the activation file, symlink and parent-directory permissions, and ACLs; a lower-privileged writer can affect a privileged shell only if that shell or a privileged task later sources it. If write access depends on sudoedit, first verify the exact sudoers rule and the installed vendor-patched sudo package; an upstream version string alone does not establish sudoedit argument-injection exposure.

Check history, dotfiles, and backups for secrets as described in users and sessions. If a privileged script resolves commands by name, combine this review with the PATH hijacking guidance.

Zsh startup redirection and compiled files

With its default RCS settings, zsh reads $ZDOTDIR/.zshenv before normal invocations, including zsh -c and scripts; if ZDOTDIR is unset, it uses $HOME. When a command runner accepts an environment map, test whether it forwards either variable into a privileged zsh process. A writable .zshenv can then run before the command body that the runner checks or allowlists. This requires the privileged process to inherit the redirected directory; zsh -f skips user startup files, but not the global zshenv (often /etc/zshenv, but distribution paths vary). The macOS zsh injection page has a minimal ZDOTDIR example.[1][2]

A newer, valid .zshenv.zwc or .zshrc.zwc is executed instead of its plaintext startup file. If you can write the startup directory, compiling a modified file and then restoring harmless-looking plaintext can leave executable code in the compiled copy. This is obscurity, not encryption. The disposable test below shows why inspecting only the text file is insufficient; it does not touch a real home directory.[1][3][4]

lab=$(mktemp -d)
printf '%s\n' 'print -r -- compiled > "$ZDOTDIR/result"' > "$lab/.zshenv"
zsh -f -c 'zcompile -R "$1"' _ "$lab/.zshenv"
printf '%s\n' 'print -r -- plaintext > "$ZDOTDIR/result"' > "$lab/.zshenv"
touch -d '2 minutes ago' "$lab/.zshenv"  # ensure the .zwc is newer
ZDOTDIR="$lab" zsh -c :
cat "$lab/result"  # compiled
zsh -f -c 'zcompile -t "$1"' _ "$lab/.zshenv.zwc"

For a real target, resolve its effective ZDOTDIR/HOME, inspect both the text and .zwc files, and check timestamps, ownership, and writable parent directories. A .zwc file must match the source file and be newer to take precedence.[1][3]
